name: Battle of Leuctra
info: The Boeotians led by the Thebans defeated Sparta and its allies at Leuctra in Boeotia on 6 July 371 BCE, after a dispute over renewing the King's Peace, and Spartan influence over Greece was shattered.

facts.place: Near Leuctra, a village in Boeotia in the territory of Thespiae, central Greece
facts.sides: The Boeotians led by the Thebans, under Epaminondas with Pelopidas commanding the Sacred Band of 300, against Sparta and its allies under King Cleombrotus I; the general modern consensus is about 7,000 Boeotian infantry and 700 cavalry against about 10,000 Peloponnesian infantry, including 700 Spartiates, and 1,000 cavalry, though the ancient sources nearly all disagree
facts.outcome: The Thebans broke the Spartan right wing, Cleombrotus was mortally wounded and the Spartans and their allies fled; Xenophon puts Spartan dead at almost 1,000, about 400 of them Spartiates.

t: Epaminondas broke with Greek custom by massing the Theban infantry in a very deep column on the left, according to Xenophon at least fifty shields deep, and set it against the Spartan right, where the king stood.
The ancient sources disagree on the numbers and on the course of the fighting, and Xenophon, the only contemporary, does not mention Epaminondas at all.
More than a quarter of Sparta's full citizens were lost, and less than a decade later Sparta had lost the Peloponnesian League and half its territory.
dyk: In 370/69 BCE a Theban-led army invaded Laconia and Messenia, the first invasion of the Spartan homeland by land in recorded history, and freed the Perioeci of Messenia and its helots from Spartan enslavement.
ev: The King's Peace ends the Corinthian War and guarantees the autonomy of Greek cities not under Persian control
The Spartan general Phoebidas seizes the Cadmea, the acropolis of Thebes
An anti-Spartan exile faction overthrows Leontiades at Thebes and moves to rebuild the Boeotian League
The Thebans refuse to let each Boeotian city sign the new peace separately, and King Cleombrotus I marches into Boeotia
The Thebans under Epaminondas defeat the Spartans and their allies at Leuctra
Thebes allies with Elis, Argos and the Arcadian League
A Theban-led army invades Laconia and Messenia and frees the Perioeci of Messenia and its helots
Thebes wins the Second Battle of Mantinea, where Epaminondas dies, and its hegemony ends

sections.background:
The Corinthian War, fought from 395 BCE between Sparta and a Persian-backed coalition of Thebes, Athens, Corinth, Argos and other allies, ended in 387/6 BCE with the King's Peace, also called the Peace of Antalcidas or the first Common Peace. It guaranteed the autonomy of all Greek cities not under Persian control. Sparta, as guarantor of the peace in Greece, used the autonomy clause to force the Thebes-dominated Boeotian League to disband. In 382 BCE the Spartan general Phoebidas seized the Theban acropolis, the Cadmea, helping the pro-Spartan Leontiades and his oligarchic supporters take control of Thebes, a clear violation of Theban autonomy.

In late 379 BCE an anti-Spartan Theban exile faction overthrew Leontiades and showed its intent to reconstitute the Boeotian League by electing four of its leaders Boeotarchs. The Boeotian War began in 378 BCE, and Sparta's attempts to regain control of Thebes and Boeotia failed in succession. A short-lived peace was agreed in 375 BCE, with renewed aggression by Thebes in 373 BCE. Thebes captured and severely damaged Plataea and Thespiae and forced their citizens into exile.

By 371 BCE both Sparta and Thebes' ally Athens were ready for peace after costly naval campaigns. Thebes, facing the prospect of fighting Sparta alone, was prepared to agree to a new treaty promising the independence of all Greek cities. At the signing the Theban ambassadors wished to sign for the whole Boeotian League, but the Spartans demanded that each Boeotian city sign independently, and the Thebans refused.
sections.forces:
Several ancient sources give numbers for the two armies, but none gives all of them and they nearly all disagree. The general modern consensus is that King Cleombrotus led approximately 10,000 Peloponnesian infantry, including 700 Spartiates (full Spartan citizens), and 1,000 cavalry, against 7,000 Boeotian infantry and 700 cavalry under the Theban commander Epaminondas, with Pelopidas in command of the elite Sacred Band of 300. Diodorus Siculus has Epaminondas lead no more than 6,000, to be joined later by 1,500 Thessalian infantry and 500 cavalry. Later sources give much higher figures for the Peloponnesians: Polyaenus 40,000 against 6,000 Thebans, Frontinus 24,000 infantry and 1,600 cavalry against 3,600 infantry and 400 cavalry.

Greek heavy infantry normally formed a phalanx, a solid rectangular mass in long files, with eight ranks thought a common depth. The most experienced troops went on the right wing. Cleombrotus drew up two wings, according to Xenophon not more than twelve men deep, with the Spartans on the right and the allies on the left. He took the king's traditional place between the first and second morai of the Spartan wing, with the hippeis, a royal bodyguard of 300 young men.

Epaminondas also formed two wings, the Thebans on one and the other Boeotians on the other. Breaking with tradition, he massed the Thebans in a very deep column on the left, opposite Cleombrotus. The other Boeotians stood in a shallower echelon, progressively further to the right and rear, facing the Spartan allies. His plan was apparently to make the outcome depend on the Thebans against the Spartans, holding back his allies. No source reports where exactly the Sacred Band stood.
sections.course:
According to Xenophon, the only contemporary source, while both sides were still arming, the Spartans' mercenary peltasts attacked Boeotian camp followers and baggage handlers who were trying to withdraw, driving them back into the Boeotian army and so making it stronger. The battle proper opened with a cavalry engagement in which the Spartan cavalry was quickly defeated. It fled back through its own infantry, disrupting the Spartan lines just as the Thebans charged. Pausanias says that Epaminondas, suspecting that some Boeotian allies, particularly the Thespians, might desert, declared that all who did not wish to fight could leave, and the Thespians and some other non-Theban Boeotians did so.

Diodorus says both sides attacked together at the sound of the trumpets, the Spartans in a crescent with their left and right advancing faster than their centre, the Theban wing at double-quick time while the weaker Boeotian wing retreated. The fighting was at first even. Cleombrotus fell, and although the Spartans recovered his body, they were forced back by the heavy column while still holding formation, and finally fled. Plutarch says Cleombrotus was extending his right wing to encircle Epaminondas, and Pelopidas charged with the 300 before the line had been closed up again.

The massed Thebans, with the Sacred Band in front, struck the Spartan right wing, mortally wounded Cleombrotus and killed many of the hippeis. The Spartan wing was pushed back, then turned and routed. Xenophon says the Spartan line held long enough for the king to be carried off alive, and the left wing gave way when it saw the right pushed back. Pausanias says the allies gave way wherever they were attacked, and that the Spartans could not retreat once their king had fallen.
sections.aftermath:
According to Xenophon the Lacedaemonians, meaning the Spartans and the Perioeci, lost almost 1,000 dead, including about 400 of the 700 Spartiates present. Boeotian losses were about 300 according to Diodorus Siculus, while Pausanias reports a total of only 47. Both sides sent messengers asking for reinforcements. A truce was agreed so that the armies could collect their dead, the Thebans set up a tropaion, and the two armies held their positions for several days.

According to Xenophon, when the Spartan messenger reached Sparta all men under sixty were mobilised and sent to Leuctra under Archidamus, son of King Agesilaus II. The Athenians dismissed the Theban messenger unanswered, but Thebes' ally Jason of Pherae in Thessaly led an army south at once. When he arrived the Thebans proposed a joint attack on the Spartan position, but Jason convinced them to be content with their victory and to let the Spartans withdraw under truce.

More than a quarter of Sparta's population of full citizens had been lost, compounding an already depleted citizen body. According to Aristotle the battle was the single blow that ended Sparta's dominance in Greece. Sparta had tried to cover up earlier battlefield losses, but at Leuctra the size of the defeat was apparent to all.
sections.sources:
Four ancient writers give accounts: Xenophon, the only contemporary, Diodorus Siculus in the later first century BCE, Plutarch around 100 CE and Pausanias in the late second century CE. Their accounts are sometimes contradictory and many particulars have been debated by scholars. Xenophon's is the most complete and has details found in no other source, but it consists less of a narrative than of reasons, some might say excuses, for the surprising Spartan defeat, and it cites an oracle and omens that pointed to a Theban victory. He says nothing of Epaminondas or of Theban tactics. No other source mentions the attack on the withdrawing camp followers or a cavalry engagement.

Diodorus and Plutarch describe Epaminondas's plan of an elite wing and a weaker wing held back, and the sources give different reasons for the disorder in the Spartan line: Xenophon the fleeing cavalry, Plutarch Cleombrotus's attempt to extend his wing. Plutarch and Cornelius Nepos are the sources for the part of Pelopidas and the Sacred Band. Köchly and Rüstow, writing in 1852, believed that Pelopidas led the Sacred Band out from the rear of the Theban column to attack the Spartan right in the flank. Hans Delbrück disputed this in 1920, finding nothing in Plutarch about a breaking out to the flank, and his rejection has found near-universal agreement among modern scholars. The view that the Sacred Band fought as an independent unit in front rests on Plutarch's remark about Pelopidas after the Battle of Tegyra in 375 BCE.
sections.legacy:
For nearly two centuries Sparta had been a Greek superpower, and in 404 BCE, after its Persian-aided victory over Athens in the Peloponnesian War, it had become the undisputed leader of the Greek world. After Leuctra its hegemony was broken. In the Peloponnese, democratic factions in cities long dominated by Sparta revived, leading to civil strife, local power struggles and shifting alliances. Less than a decade after Leuctra Sparta had lost its Peloponnesian League and half its territory.

Thebes was the principal beneficiary, and the period 371–362 BCE is widely known as the Theban hegemony. It extended its power in central Greece, and in 370 BCE allied with Elis, Argos and the Arcadian League, which had seceded from the Peloponnesian League. In the winter of 370/69 BCE a Theban-led army invaded Laconia and Messenia. Further invasions in 369 and 366 BCE won Sikyon, Achaean Pellene and all of Achaea. The Second Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE, in which Epaminondas died, marked the end of the Theban hegemony. Less than thirty years later Thebes suffered utter destruction at the hands of Alexander the Great.

The Theban victory is commonly attributed to innovations of Epaminondas: the concentration of elite forces on the left, an oblique attack, a refused right wing, forces held in reserve and the integrated use of cavalry and infantry. How revolutionary these were is debatable, but they are commonly thought to have influenced Philip II of Macedon, who lived in Thebes as a hostage between 368 and 365 BCE. Pausanias called it the most famous victory ever won by Greeks over Greeks.

summary: On 6 July 371 BCE the Thebans under Epaminondas defeated a Spartan army under King Cleombrotus at Leuctra after a dispute over renewing the King's Peace. Sparta lost its hegemony over Greece, and Thebes held the leading place for about nine years.
notes: The article's sentence that Plutarch's Peloponnesian army 'consisted of 2,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry' looks garbled against the consensus of about 10,000; I left it out.
Name misspelled 'Pleopidas' in the article, used Pelopidas.

Left out: Polyaenus's snake story, Diodorus's praise words ('glorious', 'miraculously'), the 'Thebes ... exiled citizens' details beyond the background, the article's 'Sparta superpower' phrasing kept as 'superpower' once.
Whether Spartan allies or Spartans broke first, and the Sacred Band's position, are disputed or unknown in the article.
